cards.front: In which order are grid references read?
back: Eastings, then northings.

cards.front: What does a contour line join?
back: Points of equal height.

cards.front: Which graph is most suitable for showing a relationship between two variables?
back: Scatter graph.

cards.front: What is the range of 4, 7, 9 and 15?

back: Estimating a value within the known data range.

cards.front: Name the sampling method that collects data at regular intervals.
back: Systematic sampling.

cards.front: A distance is 8 cm on a 1:50,000 map. Calculate the real distance in kilometres.
back: 1 cm represents 0.5 km.

cards.front: Explain how contour spacing shows gradient.
back: Closely spaced contours show height changing rapidly over a short distance, so the slope is steep.
Widely spaced contours show a gentle slope.

cards.front: Give two features required on a clear graph.
back: Labelled axes with units.
An even and suitable scale.

cards.front: Explain one difference between a bar chart and a histogram.
back: A bar chart represents separate categories and usually has gaps.
A histogram represents continuous grouped data, so its bars touch.

cards.front: Calculate the percentage increase from 40 to 50.
back: Increase = 10.

cards.front: Explain the difference between reliability and validity.
back: Reliability is whether repetition produces similar results.
Validity is whether the method measures what the enquiry needs.

cards.front: The values are 2, 4, 4, 5 and 10. Calculate the mean and median, and identify which better represents a typical value.
back: Median = **4**.
The median may be more representative because the high value 10 pulls up the mean.

cards.front: Explain why extrapolation is less reliable than interpolation.
back: Extrapolation predicts beyond the measured data range.
The existing trend may not continue there.
No observations are available to check the estimate directly.

cards.front: Explain one advantage and one limitation of a choropleth map.
back: It makes broad spatial patterns and regional comparisons easy to see.
Values are averaged across each area, so local variation may be hidden.

cards.front: Explain how GIS could help investigate flood risk.
back: Layers for relief, rivers, rainfall, land use and settlements can be stored.
The layers can be overlaid to identify places where hazards and people coincide.
Data can be updated and different management options compared.

cards.front: Explain how to analyse a scatter graph effectively.
back: State whether correlation is positive, negative or absent and comment on its strength.
Quote paired values or refer to the line of best fit as evidence.
Identify any anomalies.
Explain that correlation alone does not prove one variable caused the other.

cards.front: Explain why systematic sampling may be suitable along an urban transect.
back: Regular intervals give coverage from one end of the route to the other.
The rule is simple and repeatable, improving reliability.
It reduces the researcher's freedom to choose only convenient sites.
However, a repeating pattern could coincide with the interval and bias the sample.

cards.front: Explain how a geographer could improve the accuracy and reliability of river velocity measurements.
back: Measure a fixed distance carefully and use the same method at every site.
Repeat readings and calculate a mean to reduce the influence of unusual results.
Use calibrated equipment and record units consistently.
Keep the position in the channel or release method consistent where possible.
